Red flags: 2022 ruling to return two objects to the heirs of Emma Budge
- On 14 November 2022 the Restitutions Committee issued a binding opinion that The Hague City Council should return a parcel gilt goblet holder made in 1642 by Andries Grill and a Sultanabad pottery dish from the 1285 to 1400 period to the heirs of Emma Budge (Restitutions Committee).
- The then Gemeentemuseum Den Haag bought both objects in 1937 at a sale at Paul Graupe auctioneers in Berlin. Contrary to Budge's instructions the objects went under the hammer after her death, and the committee found the sale "was not a free choice", so the loss of possession was involuntary and linked to the Nazi regime (Restitutions Committee).
- The council waived the right to invoke good faith. Its website had described the objects as confiscated by the German government; research found they were sold at auction in 1937 (Restitutions Committee).
- Deputy mayor Saskia Bruines said the city "had no hesitation in following the committee's recommendations". Doede Hardeman, head of collections at the museum, said: "It is important for the museum that there is a verdict that does right by history", and that the museum was preparing to return the objects (DutchNews, 16 December 2022).

WIDER CONTEXT
- In January 2016 Nairy Baghramian withdrew her nomination for the Vincent Award, which the museum, then the Gemeentemuseum Den Haag, had organised and hosted since 2014. She cited a legal dispute between the artist Danh Vo and the collector Bert Kreuk over a work by Vo shown in an exhibition Kreuk organised at the museum, writing: "I have to question the involvement of the museum in the law case between the artist Danh Vo and the collector De Kreuk." Jutta Koether also withdrew, calling it "a personal matter" (The Art Newspaper, Anny Shaw, 8 April 2016).
- Baghramian said the museum "didn't assume a neutral stance" but "rather played an active role in this legal dispute" (ArtReview, 15 January 2016, quoting her interview with Hyperallergic). The award committee said the museum remained neutral in court and "answered questions under oath of both the judge and both parties' lawyers" (ArtReview).
- Director Benno Tempel, who chaired the jury, had testified in the case. The jury said the museum "merely witnessed" the dispute and "was never party to the dispute", found that "the recent discussion has overshadowed the intention of the award", and after consulting the Broere Foundation cancelled the 2016 award in April 2016 (The Art Newspaper, 8 April 2016).
